items.title: CloudWatch PromQL alarms now support EC2 and Application Auto Scaling
items.content_snippet: Amazon CloudWatch alarms that use Prometheus Query Language (PromQL) can now trigger Amazon EC2 and Application Auto Scaling step and simple scaling policies. You can scale your EC2 Auto Scaling groups on CloudWatch OpenTelemetry metrics using the same kind of PromQL queries you use for dashboards and alerting. items.title: Amazon OpenSearch Service now lets you validate and roll back version upgrades
items.content_snippet: Amazon OpenSearch Service now supports clone-based upgrades, which let you validate a new OpenSearch version alongside your current one and cut over to it only when you're satisfied. If you find a problem, you can cancel before you cut over or roll back afterward. With clone-based upgrades, you can move to new versions with more confidence. items.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore now offers a Web Search API
items.content_snippet: Today, AWS announces the general availability of the Web Search API on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, which lets you search the web with a single API call. Web Search on AgentCore has been available as an MCP tool through AgentCore Gateway. The new InvokeWebSearch API gives applications, custom agent loops, and data pipelines search results with no resources to create. items.title: Amazon CloudWatch Logs announces account-level retention policies
items.content_snippet: Amazon CloudWatch Logs now supports account-level retention policies, so you can use a single policy to set how long log data is kept across all or subset of log groups in an AWS account. Account-level policies allow platform and security teams to bring each log group in line with their retention standards. items.title: AWS Glue adds 100 new native connectors for popular SaaS applications
items.content_snippet: AWS Glue now supports 100 new native connectors that simplify access to data in popular SaaS and REST API-based applications. Previously, bringing data from SaaS applications into AWS required writing custom code. Now, teams can create a connection once in the AWS Glue Data Catalog and reuse it across ETL jobs with the same permissions model they already use for AWS Glue. items.title: Amazon Quick is now AWS Quick
items.content_snippet: Amazon Quick, the AI workspace built only for work, is now AWS Quick, a name that reflects the enterprise security and governance built into Quick from the start as an AWS service. The new name now appears across the Quick website, the web, desktop, and mobile apps, and AWS documentation. Existing customers don't need to take any action, and Quick works the same way it did before. Amazon Quick Sight, the business intelligence capability in Quick, is now AWS Quick Sight. items.title: Greg Brockman on how OpenAI uses frontier models for cyber defense
items.content_snippet: We’re turning lessons from defending OpenAI into practical tools for our customers. OpenAI President and Co-Founder Greg Brockman shares how we used a frontier model to identify and resolve important vulnerabilities in our own code and infrastructure. That experience is informing the tools and playbooks we’re building to help other security teams strengthen their defenses as model capabilities improve. Learn more about OpenAI’s work in cybersecurity: https://openai.com/daybreak/

items.title: How CodeRabbit uses OpenAI to review AI-generated code
items.content_snippet: CodeRabbit co-founder and CEO Harjot Gill explains how the team uses OpenAI models to help teams understand, review, and secure code produced by AI agents and decide what’s ready to ship. He also shares how CodeRabbit used Codex to ship 20x more software over 6 months with the same engineering team. Read the story: https://openai.com/index/coderabbit-codex-daybreak/

items.title: Kuken Industries searches 70 years of drawings in minutes
items.content_snippet: Kuken Industries is using the OpenAI API to help engineers search 70 years of drawings in minutes. items.title: The Agents Were Fine. Everything Around Them Broke. - Joey Wang, Harvey
items.content_snippet: After 10,000 agent-written pull requests at Harvey, the agents weren't the problem. Everything around them was. Joey Wang tells three stories from Spectre, Harvey's internal cloud agent platform: letting engineers pick their own agent while one platform owns what happens after, making every action callable so agents can drive other agents, and what broke once they did. items.title: 60% of Our Data PRs Now Merge With No Human Review - Chetas Joshi, Robinhood
items.content_snippet: Coding agents made data pipeline PRs cheap, and human review couldn't keep up. Chetas Joshi shows the hybrid reviewer agent Robinhood built for its data platform: deterministic checks run first, the model judges what scripts can't, and anything risky still goes to a person. Today about 60% of those PRs merge with no human review, saving roughly 132 engineering hours a month. He covers where they draw the line between agent and human, how they evaluate the reviewer itself, and what they got wrong

items.title: An Agent That Fixes Its Own Mistakes - Saloni Gandhi & Ziwei Guo, LinkedIn
items.content_snippet: At LinkedIn, AI agents pull together profiles, preferences, career goals and activity into an evolving picture of each member's career. items.title: Stop Chatting With Spreadsheets — Francesco Galletta & Felippe Felisola Caso, Monzo
items.content_snippet: Fast answers are easy to get. Answers you can trust with your money are harder. Francesco Galletta and Felippe Felisola Caso build a financial-analyst agent harness live, using one real problem: paying for a wedding. They show the five design principles they use for AI you can trust: shared domain, consistency, evidence, accountability and verification. They also explain why calculations belong in code instead of in the model's head. Note: the speakers work at Monzo but are not presenting on Mon

items.title: Your Self-Hosted LLM Needs to Say No - Harshul Jain & Parv Khatri, Audible & SAP
items.content_snippet: Coding agents fan out, retry and burst, and if they hit an LLM you host yourself, your inference layer will happily accept every request and bury the ones you needed first. Harshul Jain and Parv Khatri make the case for admission control: deciding what to refuse before it reaches the GPU. Drawing on a review of 55 systems papers and eight real production incidents, they share five questions to ask any admission policy before you deploy it, and a checklist you can use right away.
